title: Bookkeeper, Accountant, Fractional CFO: What Each One Actually Does for Your Business
linkedin:
You already pay a bookkeeper. You already pay an accountant. So why would you need a fractional CFO too?

It's the question we hear most often, and it's a fair one. The confusion makes sense because these three titles get thrown around loosely, and in plenty of small operations one person genuinely wears two of the hats.

But they're not competing for the same job. They're answering three completely different questions, on three completely different timeframes.

Your bookkeeper's job is accuracy about what already happened. Transactions coded, accounts reconciled, BAS lodged on time, every week, without fail.

Your accountant adds a longer lens on top of that. Compliant financial statements, a lodged tax return, sometimes a structural flag around a trust or an asset purchase. Still backward-looking. Still calendar-driven around the ATO.

A fractional CFO is answering a completely different question: given all of this accurate information, what should we actually do next? Raise the price now or next quarter? Can we afford to hire before revenue catches up? What breaks if the biggest customer starts paying 30 days late?

The pattern we see most in owner-led businesses past a few million in revenue isn't messy books. It's excellent books, with nobody set up to turn them into forward decisions.

None of this makes the other two roles less important. The best version of this is all three working together, not apart.

Fair question. Here's the short version: your bookkeeper tells you what already happened this week. Your accountant tells you what happened this year, for the ATO. A fractional CFO is the one asking what you should actually do next, before the decision is made rather than after.

Most business owners we meet already have a good bookkeeper and a good accountant, and that's exactly as it should be. But those two roles answer different questions to a fractional CFO, and the difference matters more than the overlapping job titles suggest.

Your bookkeeper keeps the weekly record accurate, from reconciliations to BAS lodgement. Your accountant turns that record into compliant financial statements and a tax return once a year. Both are backward looking by design, and both do that job well.

A fractional CFO sits above that layer and asks a forward looking question instead: given accurate numbers, what should the business actually do next about pricing, hiring, cash flow or growth? For many owner-led businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, that question has simply never had anyone dedicated to answering it.

If you have solid bookkeeping and a reliable accountant but you're still doing all the forward thinking alone late at night, that's usually the sign this fourth layer is worth exploring.
